messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 39
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: City Council Member
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 54

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try

Vignette:
At eight years old, Clara spent months bracing for the sound of the front door, though she could not explain when the dread took root. The night everything shifted began like any other. She was in the dining room, knees drawn tight to her chest beneath the heavy oak console table, when her father’s voice cracked through the house. What stayed with her most vividly was the exact rhythm of his scuffed shoes against the hardwood, the way the kitchen light caught scattered silverware, and the sharp ring of a vase hitting the wall. She could not recall how she had gotten under the table, nor could she summon any memory of the dinner hour before the shouting; those stretches of time remained absolute voids. What frightened her most was the helplessness of watching, trapped in a position she had adopted to make herself small. She had come to believe that staying perfectly still was the only way to survive. Decades later, her sense of safety had narrowed to her bedroom and the soundproofed study where she now kept her constituent files. She could not explain why she only felt secure behind those specific walls, only that crossing certain thresholds without rehearsing her escape routes left her breathless. Her work as a city council member required her to sit through public comment sessions and policy debates, spaces where she found herself unconsciously scanning every face in the chamber. She watched closely for the twitch of a jaw or a sudden lean, as if reading the air for signs that harm might return. When she finally reached home, the quiet did not bring relief. She lay in bed for hours, listening to the refrigerator hum, certain that any sudden knock would mean the past had arrived. Sleep rarely came, and when it did, it fractured hours before dawn. During zoning appeals and budget hearings, memories arrived without warning. A council member’s pen clicking against a desk, a door closing too quickly, the cadence of a raised voice—any of these could pull a moment from the past straight into the room. When they did, her shoulders would drop and her legs would tuck beneath her chair, her spine curving exactly as it had beneath the console table. The gaps in her recollection had grown into a steady habit of avoidance. She stopped accepting invitations to evening receptions, politely declining because she preferred to rest. She began arriving early to council chambers to claim a corner seat near the double doors, and she never attended the community galas her husband organized. Her husband noticed how she no longer lingered in crowded restaurants or slept on the same side of the bed when the wind howled. Her days had tightened around the boundaries she carved out, layering over years until her life fit neatly inside them. What finally brought Clara to seek help was not a single crisis, but the quiet exhaustion of maintaining those boundaries. She sat across from me on a Tuesday afternoon, her hands folded in her lap, her eyes tracing the perimeter of the office door as she spoke. She did not want to be labeled or fixed, only to understand why the past refused to stay behind her. She hoped to sleep through the night without bracing for a sound that had no name, and to walk into a crowded room without scanning for danger. What she feared most was that she would always be the child under the table, forced to watch what she could not stop, forever divided between what she could remember and the absolute dark where the rest of it had gone.
